# Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta (MN 37 (PTS MN i 251))

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta* ("The Shorter Discourse on the Ending of Craving") is the thirty-seventh discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya* [Catalog; Buswell & Lopez 2014; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Set at Sāvatthi in the Eastern Park at the Palace of Migāra's Mother, the narrative opens with Sakka, ruler of the gods in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, questioning the Buddha on how a monk achieves liberation through the destruction of craving [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. The Buddha explains the principle that nothing is worth clinging to (*sabbe dhammā nālaṁ abhinivesāya*), and that one should contemplate all feelings without attachment [Anālayo 2006; Rogell 2003; Meisig 2010]. Having overheard the teaching, the venerable Mahāmoggallāna departs bodily to the Thirty-three heaven to verify whether Sakka genuinely comprehended the instruction [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Nyanaponika et al. 2003; SuttaCentral]. Finding Sakka distracted by heavenly sense pleasures, Moggallāna shakes Sakka's celestial palace (the Vejayanta Palace) with his toe, rousing a shock of spiritual urgency (*saṁvega*) that spurs the king of the gods to recall the Dhamma [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Piya Tan 2008]. Modern commentators observe that the sutta belongs to a narrative or "story-type" category in which dramatic supernatural exploits and encounters with deities outweigh the concise doctrinal exposition [Kingsbury 2002; Sujato & Brahmali 2015].

Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral include versions in the Chinese *Madhyama Āgama* (MĀ 83), *Saṁyukta Āgama* (SĀ 505), *Ekottarika Āgama* (EĀ 19.3), an individual Chinese translation (T 47), and the Pali *Sattakanipāta* (AN 7.61) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus corroborates these cross-language relationships with matches in EĀ (T 125), SĀ (T 99), and MĀ (T 26), alongside Sanskrit matches in the *Saṅghabhedavastu* [DharmaNexus]. Textual analysis demonstrates that while the narrative core tallies with the Chinese EĀ parallel, the EĀ version renders the core detachment formula through the language of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and insubstantiality [Meisig 2010]. In Pali internal reuse, DharmaNexus identifies extensive shared material between MN 37 and AN 7.61 (§15.3–15.16), as well as significant parallels in the *Saḷāyatana Saṁyutta* (SN 35.80, §3.1–3.5), *Sakka Saṁyutta* (SN 11), *Khandha Saṁyutta* (SN 22), and *Vedanā Saṁyutta* (SN 36) [DharmaNexus].
